newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - CATEX. SEDGWICK..
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - CATEX. SEDGWICK..

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN

The completion of the first electronic transaction of the Catastrophe Risk Exchange (Catex) is significant not only in the progress of the securitisation of risk but also in the changing of work in the international insurance marketplace.

The deal is not earth shattering, but it is worthy of note in a world where insurance companies have become cautions about selling coverage in areas prone to earthquakes, hurricanes and other natural disasters after paying out billions in losses from events such as Hurricane Andrew.

The ability of insurers to trade these exposures is one way in which they can manage these risks and increase their ability to write new business. Catex is not an instant solution, but it can potentially help companies deal with their current exposure to catastrophic risk.
If Catex works and the various other electronic initiatives being planned come about, the future could see underwriters and brokers working in quite a different way.
The World Insurance Network might be used by market practitioners in the way that journalists use word processors, as risks are passed to and fro.

Those working in the London market will also have to use LIMNET, the Electronic Placing Support system at Lloyd's or one of the various claims systems. Several firms such as Marsh & McLennan also have their own internal systems.
Now we can imagine a time when underwriters will access Catex online to participate in risk securitisation deals.
Increasingly companies, executives and individuals will need to be trained to use these various technologies and recognise the opportunities and traps they present.

Progress down this road will also increase the demand for at-your-fingertips information services which enable market players to direct their market knowledge and understanding of the various systems towards new areas.
Insurance will remain a people business, but those who continue to ignore the impact of technology on the business may find it just that bit tougher to compete.
--oo0oo--
The Sedgwick joint venture with the Nikols Brichetto group shows that the concept of the strategic alliance is not dead.

Sedgwick is set to make a considerable earnings increase from the deal which creates an important broking force in southern Europe and Latin America. South America in particular has vast growth potential in the short to middle term, as the flurry of new joint ventures in the region has shown.

Such an alliance is considerably cheaper than an outright acquisition and potentially almost as lucrative. Also, the option for acquisition in the future is there if business is particularly successful.

Shareholders will be glad Sedgwick is doing something - when the latest round of merger activity broke out in the broking world, chairman Sax Riley put out some pretty big hints that it was looking for a partner. Some are disappointed that none has appeared.
But Sedgwick has for some time stated its aim to increase the proportion of its income from non-broking activities to 50 percent.

It might have been unproductive to spend a lot of money on a broker with few other strings to its bow. For the same reason, it cannot be ruled out that Sedgwick will consider buying a consultancy firm, perhaps in engineering, to help with its aim of boosting revenue from the risk management sector.
Sedgwick is still the third largest broker in the world, and assuming it does not get swallowed up by the likes of Aon, it can afford a little space to carve out its direction.
